title: Listener dies or leaves a Transaction unresolved when a reply fails to parse, a handler raises, or an unexpected exception is raised

members.title: (seeded lead)
members.claim: Listener.listener_loop catches only TimeoutError, CancelledError and ConnectionClosed. Any other exception from _receive_message (e.g. websockets ConcurrencyError, json decode error) kills the listener task silently, and in-flight sends hang.
members.evidence: (seeded by the user; not yet verified)

members.title: A response the cdp parser rejects kills the listener and leaves send() hanging forever
members.claim: tab.send(cmd) or any helper built on it (tab.evaluate, get_cookies, update_targets, get_frames). Chrome's reply has a shape the generated parser does not accept: a required field is missing or an enum value is newer than the generated protocol (Chrome version skew). The Listener pops the tx from mapper and calls tx(**message) at listener_loop line 973. Transaction.__call__ catches only StopIteration around self.__cdp_obj__.send(response['result']), so the KeyError or ValueError from from_json propagates out of __call__ and out of listener_loop. The future is never resolved. The same happens if 'result' is missing (KeyError) and on the explicit `raise ProtocolException('could not parse...')` at line 130. Result: the awaiting send() hangs with no timeout, and the listener task dies. Other in-flight commands on that connection also hang until some later send() starts a new Listener. For a session tab, events pile up in the unbounded _inbox with nothing reading them.
members.evidence: probe_parse.py against a fake CDP peer printed: 'send() HUNG (timed out after 3s) / listener done: True exception: KeyError('targetInfo') / mapper after: {}'. For the cookie: 'send() HUNG ... listener done: True exception: ValueError("'SomeFutureValue' is not a valid CookieSameSite")'. A later send worked only because send() recreates the dead listener.
members.repro_idea: Run a fake websockets peer that answers Target.getTargetInfo with {"id":N,"result":{}}, or Storage.getCookies with a cookie whose sameSite is 'SomeFutureValue'. Then call asyncio.wait_for(conn.send(cdp.target.get_target_info()), 3), which times out, and check that conn.listener.task.exception() is the KeyError or ValueError.

members.title: An exception while parsing a command response kills the Listener without failing the Transaction, so the awaiting send() hangs forever
members.claim: Any send() whose response fails parsing in Transaction.__call__ hangs forever. Causes include a generated from_json KeyError/ValueError (protocol drift, an unknown enum value) or a custom command generator as allowed by the send() docstring. Example: `def cmd(): j = yield {'method':'Runtime.evaluate','params':{'expression':'1'}}; return j['x']`, then `await tab.send(cmd())` never returns. `tx(**message)` runs outside every try block. The exception escapes listener_loop, the task dies with 'Task exception was never retrieved', and tx (already popped from mapper) is never set_result/set_exception'd. Any concurrent tab.wait() blocked on that listener's idle event also hangs. This is a different site from the known issue: that issue covers the try around _receive_message, and here the receive succeeded and the response dispatch is what fails.
members.evidence: probe_fake.py (fake peer, generated cdp.runtime.evaluate) printed "C: send() hung; listener running: False listener exc: KeyError('exceptionId')". probe_parse.py (real Chromium, custom generator) printed 'send() HUNG: timed out after 5s instead of raising KeyError', old listener task exception 'notThere', mapper size 0 (tx popped but never completed).
members.repro_idea: Use a fake websockets.serve peer that answers Runtime.evaluate with {'id':n,'result':{'result':{'type':'object'},'exceptionDetails':{'bogus':1}}}. `await asyncio.wait_for(conn.send(cdp.runtime.evaluate('1')), 3)` times out instead of raising KeyError. The fix is to wrap tx(**message) and set_exception on the tx.

members.title: A command reply that fails to parse kills the Listener, and the send() waiting for it hangs forever (aclose() cannot release it either)
members.claim: Any tab.send()/connection.send() whose result the generated cdp parser rejects. This happens when Chrome's protocol differs from the bundled cdp: a required key is missing (KeyError), or there is a new enum value, e.g. a cookie sameSite value unknown to CookieSameSite (ValueError). listener_loop pops the Transaction from conn.mapper and then calls tx(**message) outside any try. Inside Transaction.__call__, cdp_obj.send(result) raises something other than StopIteration, and the exception leaves listener_loop, so the listener task dies. The Future is never resolved. It is already gone from mapper, so _fail_pending_transactions in aclose()/_detach_session can never fail it, and send() hangs forever. Its own explicit `raise ProtocolException('could not parse the cdp response')` also kills the listener instead of failing the tx. On the browser connection this also starves every flat-session tab, because no one reads the websocket until another browser-level send() creates a new Listener. Event parsing on the same loop does catch these errors (parse_json_event in try/except -> logger.info; continue), which shows the intended behaviour.
members.evidence: probe_tx_parse.py printed: 'send done within 3s: False | listener running: False | listener exc: KeyError('targetInfo')' with the task stuck at connection.py:662 `return await tx`. The same happened for Storage.getCookies with sameSite 'SomeFutureValue': listener exc ValueError("'SomeFutureValue' is not a valid CookieSameSite"). probe_tx_parse2.py: 'after aclose(): send finished? False | tx in mapper: 0'. The only trace is 'Task exception was never retrieved' at GC. Related to the known 'listener only catches Timeout/Cancelled/ConnectionClosed' lead, but this site is outside that try. The fix belongs in result dispatch (tx.set_exception), and the tx is lost permanently.

Call conn.send(cdp.target.get_target_info()) as a task, wait 3s, then call conn.aclose() and check that the task is still pending. Probe: /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-zendriver/b2021b39-94e6-5220-9e66-7f33c0314a80/scratchpad/detect-B15/probe_tx_parse.py and probe_tx_parse2.py

members.title: One event handler that raises when called (e.g. wrong arity) kills the Listener through an explicit re-raise, so commands already in flight hang
members.claim: A user registers `async def on_target(): ...` (no parameters) via browser.connection.add_handler(cdp.target.TargetCreated, on_target) or tab.add_handler(...). _accepts_connection_argument returns False, so the loop calls callback(event), which raises TypeError synchronously while the coroutine object is created. The dispatch block logs a warning and then `raise`s (the outer `except Exception: raise` passes it on too), so the listener task dies. The reply to a command that is already in flight, and is queued right behind the event, is never read: that send() hangs until some later send() happens to create a new Listener. Every other handler for every event also stops firing. On the browser connection this starves all flat-session tabs, since nothing reads the shared websocket.
members.evidence: probe_bad_handler.py printed: 'get_version finished within 3s: False' and 'listener running: False exc: TypeError('main.<locals>.bad_handler() takes 0 positional arguments but 1 was given')'. This is a distinct site from the known receive-side lead: the loop raises on purpose after logging, rather than isolating the faulty callback.
members.repro_idea: Run a fake CDP peer that, for Browser.getVersion, first sends a Target.targetCreated event and then the reply. Register a good handler plus `async def bad(): pass`, then call conn.send(cdp.browser.get_version()) with a 3s timeout. Probe: /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-zendriver/b2021b39-94e6-5220-9e66-7f33c0314a80/scratchpad/detect-B15/probe_bad_handler.py

members.title: Once the browser connection's Listener stops, every flat-session Tab command hangs because the tab path never restarts the parent listener
members.claim: After browser.connection.listener dies (for example from the response-parse failure above on a browser-level command, or from the known ConcurrencyError), `await tab.send(cdp.runtime.evaluate('1'))` and `await tab.evaluate('1+1')` hang forever. For a Tab, aopen() calls only _attach_session(), which returns early when session_id is set and never calls browser_connection.aopen(). send() then restarts only the tab's own Listener, which reads tab._inbox. Nothing reads the websocket, so nothing fills that inbox. A self-heal exists for the browser connection (send restarts its listener), but tab traffic never reaches it. Tabs recover only when unrelated code happens to send on browser.connection.
members.evidence: probe_parse2.py printed: 'browser.connection.send HUNG instead of raising KeyError', 'browser listener running: False', 'tab.send HUNG too: tab listener running: True inbox size 0', 'tab.evaluate HUNG', then 'after a browser-level send, tab send ok: 6'. Confidence is medium only because the trigger depends on a listener death, which is either the known issue or the finding above. The missing revival is a separate defect.
members.repro_idea: Real Chromium: `await asyncio.wait_for(browser.connection.send(bad_custom_cmd()), 5)` (it times out and the browser listener dies). Then `await asyncio.wait_for(tab.send(cdp.runtime.evaluate('2+2')), 5)` also times out. After `await browser.connection.send(cdp.target.get_targets())`, the tab send works again. The fix is to have the flat-session aopen ensure that the parent's listener is running.

files: zendriver/core/connection.py (Transaction.__call__, Listener.listener_loop, Connection.send/aopen for session tabs)
fix: Make Transaction.__call__ set_exception on the future for any parse error instead of raising; in listener_loop isolate per-callback dispatch errors (log, do not re-raise) and handle unexpected exceptions from _receive_message without silently dying (fail pending transactions so callers do not hang); make a flat-session tab's send/aopen restart the parent browser connection's listener when it is not running.
test: Browser-free: fake websocket/peer that replies with a result the generated parser rejects (missing key / unknown enum) -> send() raises within a bound instead of hanging; handler with wrong arity -> later sends still answered; parent listener dead -> tab send still answered.

title: Polling methods that take a timeout (find/select/find_all/select_all/xpath/wait_for/tab()/verify_cf/cf_* helpers) do not bound their CDP awaits, so they hang forever when the renderer does not answer (alert() open, busy JS)

members.title: Tab.find/select/find_all/select_all ignore their timeout when one CDP reply never comes, so they hang forever on a page blocked by a dialog or busy JS
members.claim: tab = browser.main_tab; await tab.get(page); the page then runs alert('x') or a busy loop `while(true){}` (from a setTimeout, an anti-bot script, etc.). await tab.select('#nope', timeout=2) never returns. The same happens with find('x', timeout=2), find_all(..., timeout=2) and select_all(..., timeout=2). Each loop pass awaits query_selector/find_elements_by_text -> self.send(DOM.getDocument), which the blocked renderer never answers. The timeout is only compared after the await returns (`if loop.time() - start_time > timeout`), so it is never checked. include_frames=True adds more unbounded sends (get_frames, per-frame searches), and self.sleep(0.5) adds one more (update_target). This is the same defect fixed for wait_for_ready_state in bd88ccd (#291, 'page stuck behind a dialog'), but the fix was not applied to these methods.

In both 'busy' (while(true){}) and 'alert' modes it printed e.g. `busy select: STILL PENDING after 15.0s (timeout=2)` with the stack `Tab.select() running at tab.py:351 wait_for=<Transaction method: DOM.getDocument status: pending>`. Same for find (tab.py:308), find_all (tab.py:382) and select_all (tab.py:423). In the same conditions wait_for_ready_state(timeout=2) correctly raised TimeoutError after 2.0s, and tab.wait(2) returned after 2.0s.

members.title: select/find/find_all/select_all/xpath ignore their timeout when a CDP reply never comes (open alert() or busy renderer): hang forever
members.claim: A page opens a JS dialog (setTimeout(()=>alert('x'),100)) or runs a long synchronous script. Then `await tab.select('#missing', timeout=2)` never returns. The loop checks `loop.time() - start_time > timeout` only between attempts, and each attempt awaits `self.send(cdp.dom.get_document(...))` (query_selector line 638, find_elements_by_text line 697) with no deadline. The renderer main thread does not answer DOM.getDocument while the dialog is open. `tab.find('x', timeout=2)` hangs the same way. `tab.xpath('//x', timeout=1)`, whose docstring says 'It will not raise', hangs on `await self.send(cdp.dom.enable(), True)` (line 473). find_all and select_all use the same loop structure, and include_frames adds unbounded per-frame sends.

members.title: Tab.wait_for / tab(...) / Tab.xpath hang forever past their timeout when the renderer stops answering
members.claim: await tab.wait_for(selector='#x', timeout=2), or await tab(selector='#x', timeout=2), on a page blocked by alert() or a busy loop. The first query_selector before the while loop, and each one inside it, awaits DOM.getDocument with no bound; `loop.time() - start_time < timeout` is only checked after it returns, so the documented 'block for a maximum of <timeout> seconds, then TimeoutError' never happens. Tab.xpath(xpath, timeout=2.5), documented to return [] after the timeout and 'never raise', likewise hangs on its per-pass `await self.send(cdp.dom.enable(), True)` and find_all(timeout=0).

members.title: Tab.wait_for's timeout does not bound query_selector/find_element_by_text: it hangs forever while a JS dialog is open and overshoots on a busy page
members.claim: A page shows alert() (or any JS dialog) and the caller does await tab.wait_for(selector='#x', timeout=2) or tab.wait_for(text='x', timeout=2). The timeout is only checked in the while condition between iterations. The first query_selector call sends DOM.getDocument, which Chrome does not answer while the dialog is open, so wait_for never returns and never raises TimeoutError. The documented contract is 'it will block for a maximum of <timeout> seconds, after which a TimeoutError will be raised'. On a page whose main thread is busy for 12s, wait_for(timeout=2) returns only after about 11.3s. wait_for_ready_state was fixed for exactly this in #291 (CHANGELOG line 27), but wait_for was not.

members.title: verify_cf / cf_is_interactive_challenge_present timeout does not bound their CDP calls, so they hang on a blocked page instead of raising or returning False

Each pass of cf_wait_for_interactive_challenge awaits cf_find_interactive_challenge -> tab.send(DOM.getDocument), plus get_html() for each shadow root, all with no bound. `while loop.time() - start_time < timeout` is only checked after they return. members.title: verify_cf timeout is overrun by up to click_delay (and by any slow CDP call) although the docstring says it governs the total time
members.claim: The deadline is checked only at the top of the click loop (line 254). Each iteration then does mouse_click, an unbounded `asyncio.sleep(click_delay)` (line 260), and check_input (getDocument + resolveNode + another getDocument), none of which is bounded by the remaining time. So tab.verify_cf(timeout=1, click_delay=4) on an unsolvable challenge takes about 4s. With the defaults (timeout=15, click_delay=5), a challenge found near the deadline runs about 20s. cf_wait_for_interactive_challenge has the same issue: every full DOM scan (getDocument plus one getOuterHTML per shadow root) runs to completion past the deadline, so cf_is_interactive_challenge_present(tab, timeout=5) can take far longer than 5s, and forever if a CDP reply never comes. This is a different site from the known Tab.get/Browser.get issue.

members.title: xpath(timeout=0) (or any timeout <= 0) never runs the query and always returns []; otherwise it busy-loops with no sleep
members.claim: `await tab.xpath("//p[@id='topp']", timeout=0)` returns [] although the element exists. The loop condition `(loop.time() - start_time) < timeout and len(items) == 0` is checked before the first attempt, so with timeout <= 0 the body never runs. The docstring says retries happen only 'if not immediately found', implying at least one attempt. With a positive timeout the loop has no sleep between attempts (find_all(timeout=0) raises immediately, the exception is caught, and the loop spins). One miss with timeout=0.5 issued 1254 Tab.send calls, each attempt including a full-tree DOM.getDocument(depth=-1, pierce=True).

title: Browser.stop()/_stop()/_atexit_cleanup cleanup is not robust: unbounded CDP awaits before terminate/kill, exceptions from Tab.aclose abort cleanup, concurrent stop() crashes, and the atexit path fails at asyncio.to_thread after the executor is shut down

members.title: Browser.stop() waits on unbounded CDP replies before it kills the process, so an unresponsive browser makes stop() hang forever and leaks the process
members.claim: When the browser process stops answering (e.g. the stderr-pipe deadlock above, a wedged or suspended Chrome, a remote browser that hangs), await browser.stop() never returns. _stop first runs `await target.aclose()` for every target. For each attached flat session that does `await browser_connection.send(Target.detachFromTarget)` with no timeout. It then does `await self.connection.send(cdp.browser.close())`, also with no timeout. Only after both does it reach the terminate -> 3 s -> kill fallback, which is the code meant for an unresponsive browser. If the caller bounds stop() with asyncio.wait_for, the process is never terminated and the temp profile is never removed. stop() already called asyncio_atexit.unregister(self._atexit_cleanup) and discarded the instance from the registry before awaiting _stop(), so nothing cleans up at exit either. Tab.close() has the same shape: its `await self.browser.connection.send(close_target)` sits outside the `asyncio.wait_for(future, 10)` that its ':raises asyncio.TimeoutError:' docstring promises.
members.evidence: probe_stop.py: `stop() STILL PENDING after 20.0s; process alive: True`, stack `Browser.stop() running at browser.py:872 wait_for=<Transaction method: Target.detachFromTarget status: pending>`. The pipe-deadlock probe also showed `stop failed TimeoutError` with an outer 15 s wait_for. The websocket ping_timeout is 900 s, so the connection would not even fail on its own for over 15 minutes.
members.repro_idea: browser = await zd.start(headless=True); tab = await browser.get(url); await tab.evaluate('1') to attach a session; os.kill(pid, SIGSTOP); then assert asyncio.wait_for(browser.stop(), 20) completes and the process is gone. Fix: bound the detach/Browser.close steps (e.g. wait_for of a few seconds each, or overall) and always fall through to terminate/kill.

members.title: Browser.stop() hangs forever on an unresponsive browser and never reaches terminate()/kill()
members.claim: The Chrome process is wedged: frozen, stopped, or blocked writing to its full stderr pipe (see the pipe finding). `await browser.stop()` first runs `for target in self.targets: await target.aclose()`, and each aclose sends Target.detachFromTarget over the browser connection with no timeout. Next comes `await self.connection.send(cdp.browser.close())`, also with no timeout. The websocket stays open but no reply ever arrives, so stop() blocks forever. The terminate/kill block, which exists to handle a stubborn process, is never reached. The obvious workaround, `asyncio.wait_for(browser.stop(), t)`, makes things worse: stop() has already unregistered the atexit callback and removed the instance from the registry before awaiting _stop(), so after the timeout nothing will ever kill Chrome or remove the temp profile.

members.repro_idea: `b = await zd.start(headless=True); await b.get('about:blank'); os.kill(b._process_pid, SIGSTOP); t = asyncio.create_task(b.stop()); await asyncio.wait({t}, timeout=12)`. t is still pending and t.print_stack() shows it waiting on the Target.detachFromTarget Transaction.

members.title: Browser.stop() hangs forever on an unresponsive browser, because the CDP detach/close steps have no timeout and the terminate/kill fallback comes after them
members.claim: The Chrome browser process stops responding (hung or suspended) and the user calls `await browser.stop()`. _stop first awaits `target.aclose()` for every target. For attached tabs that sends Target.detachFromTarget through the browser connection and awaits the reply with no timeout. Then it awaits `self.connection.send(cdp.browser.close())`, also with no timeout. The 3s terminate -> kill fallback is never reached, so stop() never returns. If the caller wraps it in wait_for, the cancellation leaves the process running and the profile undeleted.

members.claim: Start a browser and use a tab, which attaches a flat session. The Chrome process then stops answering: it is hung, SIGSTOPped, or blocked on the full stderr pipe. Calling await browser.stop() first runs asyncio_atexit.unregister (line 870). _stop then awaits target.aclose() for each target (each sends Target.detachFromTarget through the browser connection) and connection.send(Browser.close), and none of these awaits has a timeout. stop() hangs forever and never reaches self._process.terminate()/kill(). If the caller wraps stop() in wait_for, the cancel leaves the process running and the temp profile in place, and because the atexit hook is already gone, nothing cleans up later.

members.title: Browser.stop() right after Chrome dies raises ConnectionClosedError from Tab.aclose and leaks the process and temp profile
members.claim: browser = await zd.start(); tab = await browser.get(...); await tab.evaluate('1') (the tab now has a flat session). members.title: Chrome's stdout/stderr are PIPEs that are never drained: once ~64 KiB of logs pile up, Chrome blocks and every CDP call (and stop()) hangs
members.claim: zd.start() spawns Chrome with stdout=PIPE and stderr=PIPE. Nothing reads them during the session; only _read_process_stderr does, and only after start() fails to connect. Chrome logs ERROR lines to stderr. Default flags in a container already leave about 5 KB at startup (dbus errors), and each navigation that hits a certificate error adds about 370 bytes. When the 64 KiB kernel pipe buffer fills, the Chrome thread that logs blocks in write(2). From then on: (a) default flags: after about 157 bad-certificate navigations, Page.navigate is never answered, so tab.get / tab.send / find etc. hang; (b) with a common debugging flag such as browser_args=['--enable-logging=stderr','--v=1'], the browser process stops answering even Browser.getVersion within a few navigations, and browser.stop() hangs too (see the stop() finding). The user sees a browser that just stops responding, with no error.

members.title: expect_request/expect_response: buffered matching events overwrite request_id, so .response and .response_body come from a different request than .value
members.claim: async with tab.expect_request(r'.*/pix\d+\.gif') as exp: await tab.get(page_with_30_images); req = await exp.value; resp = await exp.response. Chrome sends several Network.requestWillBeSent frames in one read. On Python >= 3.12, Listener.listener_loop drains buffered websocket frames without yielding: wait_for no longer creates a task, and websockets' SimpleQueue.get does not suspend when data is queued. So it calls asyncio.create_task(_request_handler(ev)) once per matching event before the first task runs and removes the handler. The first task sets request_future to request R1. Every later task overwrites self.request_id with its own id (Rn), and its request_future.set_result raises InvalidStateError inside an unobserved task. _response_handler then matches Rn. The result: exp.value / exp.request describe pix0.gif, while exp.response, exp.response_body and loading_finished_future describe pix9.gif (for example). BaseFetchInterception._response_handler and DownloadExpectation._handler have the same unguarded set_result, which produces the lost InvalidStateError tasks.

Sample: 'value.url=pix0.gif request_id(attr)=28835.11 value.request_id=28835.2 response.url=pix9.gif match=False'. The loop exception handler caught 55 lost InvalidStateError('invalid state') task exceptions.

It then reads the next buffered frame without yielding, because wait_for awaits the coroutine inline and websockets returns buffered frames immediately. That frame is Target.detachedFromTarget, so _receive_message calls session._detach_session(). That sets self._inbox = None, which drops the queued reply, and fails every pending tx with ProtocolException('target session was detached'). The command succeeded in Chrome, but the caller sees a failure. The comment in Tab.close ('sent through the browser session, since this tab's own session may be detached before chrome responds') works around exactly this for close_target, but every other session command is still exposed. A fix would drain the inbox (or deliver the detach through the inbox) before failing the pending txs.

The control probe_detach_race_delay.py, with a 50ms gap between reply and detach, printed 'caller saw success: 20, saw ProtocolException: 0'. On real Chromium with page.close / target.close via the session, the frames arrived separately in 6 trials, so the bug did not show there.

Then asyncio.wait_for(tab.evaluate('1+1'), small_timeout), or any timeout or cancel that hits the first send. _attach_session has already sent Target.attachToTarget and is awaiting the reply when it is cancelled. Chrome creates the session, but self.session_id is never set and the id is never recorded in browser_connection._sessions. The next send attaches a second session. tab.aclose() and Browser.stop() later detach only the recorded session, so the orphaned DevTools session stays attached in Chrome until the browser websocket closes. Each timed-out first command leaks one.

members.claim: tab.send(...) on a target that is being destroyed: for example an OOPIF from get_frames() whose iframe is removed, or a tab closed concurrently. aopen -> _attach_session awaits browser_connection.send(Target.attachToTarget). Chrome sends the attach reply and then Target.detachedFromTarget for the new session. On Python >= 3.12 the browser listener handles both buffered frames before _attach_session resumes. _receive_message finds no entry in _sessions for that id, so the detach is ignored. Then _attach_session registers browser_connection._sessions[sid] = self and keeps session_id=sid. Every later command on the tab goes out with the dead sessionId. Chrome's reply for an unknown session carries no sessionId (verified against real Chromium: {"id":4,"error":{"code":-32001,"message":"Session with given id not found."}}). The reply is therefore routed to the browser connection, whose mapper does not contain the id, and silently dropped. tab.send has no timeout of its own, so this send and every later send on that tab hang forever.

The first start() wrote host='127.0.0.1' and port=free_port() into self.config. stop() clears _process and _process_pid but not host or port. So the second start() sees host and port both set and sets connect_existing=True: no executable check, no process spawn. test_connection then fails every retry against the dead port. members.title: Forwarder leaks tunnels to an authenticated https:// upstream after Chrome closes the connection, because the close is never passed upstream
members.claim: Call browser.create_context(proxy_server='https://user:pass@proxy:443'), browse, then let Chrome close a tunnelled connection (tab or context closed, idle socket dropped). copy_stream(client->upstream) reads EOF and calls write_eof() only if writer.can_write_eof(). An asyncio SSL transport returns False there, so the upstream proxy is never told and the tunnel stays up. pipe() gathers both directions, so it keeps waiting for upstream->client to reach EOF. Meanwhile the _handle_client task, the half-open client socket, the TLS upstream socket, the upstream proxy's tunnel and the origin connection all stay alive until the remote side times out (minutes for TLS or HTTP/2 origins, since Chromium does not send close_notify). With an http:// or socks5 upstream the FIN is forwarded and everything is torn down at once. Long scraping sessions through https proxies pile up these connections.
members.evidence: Scratch proxy_probe.py: 'tls=False: forwarder client tasks still alive 2s after client closed: 0' and 'tls=True: forwarder client tasks still alive 2s after client closed: 1', with the same fake proxy and origin in both runs. The only difference is the TLS upstream.
members.repro_idea: Run a TLS CONNECT proxy (self-signed cert) whose origin closes on EOF. Build ProxyForwarder(UpstreamProxy.from_url('https://u:p@127.0.0.1:port', insecure_ctx)), open a CONNECT tunnel, close the client socket, sleep 2s, then check len(forwarder._client_tasks).

members.title: Proxy forwarder drops the client connection without an HTTP error, and logs an unhandled-exception traceback, when encoding or parsing raises something other than ProxyError
members.claim: _handle_client turns only ProxyError into an HTTP error response, and silently handles only OSError, IncompleteReadError and LimitOverrunError. With a socks5 upstream, a CONNECT or GET to a host that has a DNS label over 63 characters or an empty label (e.g. 'a..b.com') makes encode_socks5_address raise UnicodeError from host.encode('idna') (line 337). open_tunnel re-raises it unchanged, _handle_client lets it escape, the client gets an empty response instead of the 502 used for every other upstream failure, and asyncio logs 'ERROR asyncio: Unhandled exception in client_connected_cb' with a full traceback. ValueError from urlsplit or url.port on malformed targets (non-CONNECT path, line 263/274) goes the same way.
members.evidence: Scratch proxy_probe.py: 'LOG ERROR asyncio: Unhandled exception in client_connected_cb ... UnicodeEncodeError: 'idna' codec can't encode characters in position 0-63: label too long' and 'long-label CONNECT response: b'''. Expected was 'HTTP/1.1 502 Proxy Error'.
members.repro_idea: With a socks5 upstream forwarder, send `CONNECT {'a'*64}.example.com:443 HTTP/1.1\r\n\r\n` and read the response.

members.title: open_tunnel reports a timed-out proxy handshake as 'proxy closed the connection' because TimeoutError is an OSError subclass
members.claim: On Python 3.11+, asyncio.TimeoutError is the builtin TimeoutError, which subclasses OSError. The isinstance(e, (OSError, IncompleteReadError)) check at line 112 therefore matches first, and the `isinstance(e, asyncio.TimeoutError)` branch at line 114 can never run. When an upstream proxy accepts TCP but never answers CONNECT or the SOCKS handshake within TIMEOUT, the warning logged by _handle_client says 'proxy closed the connection: TimeoutError()' instead of 'timed out waiting for the proxy', which misleads anyone debugging a slow proxy. The status (502) is the same.
members.evidence: Scratch proxy_probe.py on Python 3.13.16: 'handshake timeout -> 'proxy closed the connection: TimeoutError()''.
members.repro_idea: Set zendriver.core.proxy.TIMEOUT=0.5 and point UpstreamProxy at a server that accepts and never replies. Call open_tunnel('example.com', 443) and print str(ProxyError).

title: ContraDict semantics: update/setdefault/|= store plain dicts; copy.copy/pickle keep stale attributes after del; assigning an existing ContraDict/list stores a copy

members.title: ContraDict.update(), setdefault() and |= store plain dicts unconverted, so nested attribute access breaks
members.claim: The docstring promises 'recursive action. dict assignments will be converted too', but only __setitem__ and __setattr__ run _wrap. dict.update, dict.setdefault and dict.__ior__ on a subclass do not call __setitem__. So `cd = zendriver.cdict(); cd.update({'a': {'b': 1}}); cd.a.b` raises AttributeError: 'dict' object has no attribute 'b'. The same happens with cd.setdefault('s', {'b': 1}) and `cd |= {'o': {'b': 1}}`. ContraDict and cdict are exported in zendriver.__all__, and Element.attrs and Browser.info are ContraDicts that users may update.
members.evidence: Scratch cd_probe.py: 'after update, c2.a.b -> RAISES AttributeError', 'after setdefault, c2.s.b -> RAISES AttributeError', 'after |=, c2.o.b -> RAISES AttributeError'.
members.repro_idea: c = ContraDict(); c.update({'a': {'b': 1}}); c.a.b

members.title: copy.copy() or pickling a ContraDict gives an object that still returns deleted keys as attributes
members.claim: __init__ makes the instance __dict__ the dict itself (`super().__setattr__('__dict__', self)`). copy.copy and pickle rebuild through __reduce_ex__ without calling __init__: they create a separate real __dict__ and copy every item into it as state (the state is the dict itself), then set the items again. After `c = copy.copy(cd); del c['a']`, `'a' in c` is False but `c.a` still returns the old value, because __getattribute__ falls through to object.__getattribute__, which finds the stale entry in the separate __dict__. `c.pop('a')` behaves the same, and vars(c) is stale. This affects e.g. copy.copy(element.attrs), copy.copy(browser.info), or a ContraDict sent through multiprocessing.
members.evidence: Scratch cd_probe.py: 'after del c5['a'] (copy.copy), c5.a -> {'b': 1}', 'after del c7['a'], c7.a -> {'b': 1}' (pickle), 'vars(copy) is copy -> False'. deepcopy is not affected (memo makes the state the new object).
members.repro_idea: c = copy.copy(ContraDict({'a': {'b': 1}})); del c['a']; print(c.a)  # prints {'b': 1} instead of raising AttributeError. pickle.loads(pickle.dumps(...)) does the same.

members.title: Assigning an existing ContraDict or list to a ContraDict stores a copy, so later changes to the original are not seen
members.claim: _wrap always rebuilds mappings (cls(v)) and non-str sequences (a new list), even when v is already a ContraDict or a list. So `inner = cdict(); cd.child = inner; inner.x = 1; cd.child` gives {} and `cd.child is inner` is False. Likewise `lst = []; cd.l = lst; lst.append(1); cd.l` gives []. Plain dict assignment keeps the reference, which the docstring ('directly inherited from dict') suggests is also what ContraDict does. copy.copy() also turns into a deep copy for nested mappings (c.a is not cd.a).
members.evidence: Scratch cd_probe.py: 'c3.child after inner.x=1 -> {}', 'c3.l after lst.append -> []', 'copy.copy is shallow? c5.a is c4.a -> False'.
members.repro_idea: inner = ContraDict(); c = ContraDict(); c.child = inner; inner.x = 1; assert c.child == {}  # surprising

fix: Override update/setdefault/__ior__; fix __reduce__/copy; avoid rewrapping.
test: Browser-free.

members.title: tab.intercept() cannot be nested or combined with other Fetch users: inner enable replaces the outer patterns, the outer handler takes the inner request, and the inner teardown makes Fetch re-enable with no patterns, pausing every request
members.claim: (1) `async with tab.intercept('*a.json*', REQUEST, XHR) as a: async with tab.intercept('*b.json*', REQUEST, XHR) as b: await tab.get(page_fetching_a_and_b)`. The inner Fetch.enable([b]) replaces the tab's pattern list, so a.json is never paused. _response_handler accepts any Fetch.requestPaused without checking its own pattern, so both a and b resolve with b.json. `await a.request` returns b.json, `a.continue_request()` continues b's request, and `b.continue_request()` raises ProtocolException. (2) The inner block exits before the outer one has matched: _teardown sends Fetch.disable, which turns off interception for the whole tab and removes fetch from manually_enabled_domains. The outer RequestPaused handler is still registered, so the next tab.send() goes through Connection._register_handlers, which sends `fetch.enable()` with no patterns. Every request, including the document, now pauses. `tab.get()` hangs, the outer interception resolves with the page document instead of a.json, and the page's XHRs never complete. The same happens when a user-installed RequestPaused handler with its own Fetch.enable coexists with tab.intercept().
